column11: Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 670:2: “Taz (Orach Chayim 670:3, citing the Levush) explains why Purim has an obligation of festive meals (mishteh ve-simchah) whereas Chanukah’s primary obligation is Hallel and praise rather than feasting: on Purim Haman decreed to annihilate the physical bodies of Israel, so the salvation is celebrated with bodily feasting; on Chanukah the Greeks sought to uproot the soul and the Torah while leaving the body intact if Israel assimilated, so the salvation is celebrated through spiritual praise and the light of Torah.” Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 9, Rav Tzadok cites this commentary and philosophical-halakhic exposition (Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 670:2) to illuminate his exposition here (“And the Taz (Section 670, subsection 3) cited from the Levush that on Purim physical salvation occurred, and therefore it contains a mitzvah of feasting, unlike Chanukah where the Greeks decreed...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.

column11: Sotah 21a: ‘And the Torah is associated with light in order to say to you: Just as the light of the sun protects one forever, so too, the Torah one studies protects one forever; and it states in the previous verse with regard to the Torah: “When you walk, it shall lead you; when you lie down, it shall watch over you; and when you awake, it shall talk with you” (Proverbs 6:22). The Gemara explains: “When you walk, it shall lead you”; this is referring to when one is in this world. “When you lie down, it shall watch over you”; this is referring to the time of death, when one lies in his grave. “And when you awake, it shall talk with you”; this is referring to the time to come after the resurrection of…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 10, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sotah 21a) to illuminate his exposition here (“and when you awake it shall talk with you — in the Future to Come" (Sotah 21a); for then, at the Resurrection of the Dead, the ultimate clarification in this will emerge, showing that death was...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And it is said: “And you shall come unto the priests the Levites, and unto the judge”; and in Torah there is sweet fragrance, in the idiom of our Sages: “the scent of Torah”, because scent is perceived from afar, and so the Torah protects even when one is not actively studying it, as written in Sotah 21a; and fragrant scent is beneficial to neighbors, as they compared in Eruvin 17b and Yoma to kerosene and balsam.
column15: “By His knowledge the depths were broken open”—the concept of the abyss (tehom) was already explained above (section 5) as referring to the treasury of blessings that Hashem will bestow in the World to Come.

column11: Shabbat 149b: ‘Rather, the basis for this idea is from here: “Punishment is also not good for the righteous” (Proverbs 17:26), meaning that it is not good for a righteous person to issue punishment. There is no meaning of not good other than evil. And it says: “For You are not a God that desires wickedness, evil will not dwell with You” (Psalms 5:5), meaning that You, God, are righteous and evil shall not dwell with You in Your place of dwelling. Even a righteous person who punishes someone and is called evil and cannot dwell within God’s partition.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 10, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 149b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and they said (Shabbat 149b): "You are righteous, Hashem, and evil does not reside in Your dwelling", which withholds the resting of the Shechinah as it were, and as written in the Zohar (ibid.)...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: Since he served as the direct catalyst for his fellow's demise, and our Sages said: "Even the stone used for stoning is destined to be judged"; and this appears contrary to human intellect, for what else could he have done? Rather, in this subtle realm is ensnared specifically one attached to the transcendent root that surpasses intellect, and therefore David was likewise held to task when God said to him: "Through you, etc."; yet since David's concealed root was purely good, he incurs no destruction.
column15: My revered father, of blessed memory, explained: How can such phrasing apply to Hashem, as if only now He realized that it is not good for man to be alone, whereas prior to creation He had not foreseen this? Rather, this very condition was itself a deliberate act of creation by Hashem: that man should feel he finds no helper — meaning that within his own human perception, no immediate aid should be apparent.

column11: Zohar, Vayechi 23:182-26:195: ‘R. Judah said: ‘Every sin admits of repentance barring this, and every sinner may hope to see the face of the Shekinah barring this one.’ R. Isaac said: ‘Happy are the righteous in this world and in the world to come; of them it is written: “And thy people are all righteous, they shall for ever inherit the land (Is. 60, 21). on Leviticus, 104b, to which they properly belong.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 10, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Vayechi 23:182-26:195) to illuminate his exposition here (“and as written in the Zohar (ibid.) that he does not gaze upon the Face of the Shechinah. However, through the rectification it is stated: "The eyes of Hashem are toward the righteous, etc.", and...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: But there prior to this they explained regarding his punishment that "he does not behold the countenance of the Shechinah"; and likewise [in Parashas Vayeshev there] that "he does not enter and does not gaze upon the pleasant countenance of the Ancient of Days"; and likewise [in Parashas Bereishis 57a] that "he does not enter the royal palace (palterin) and does not behold the countenance of the Shechinah"; and likewise [in Parashas Emor 90a, start of s.v. v'la].
column15: When we see that the yearning of that person is to pursue and exert himself after the Holy One, blessed be He, with his heart, his soul, and his will, we know with certainty that the Shechinah rests upon him.

column11: Shabbat 22b: ‘Rav Sheshet raised an objection from that which was taught in a baraita. With regard to the Temple candelabrum, it is stated: “Outside the veil of the testimony, in the Tent of Meeting, shall Aaron order it from evening to morning before the Lord continually; it shall be a statute forever throughout your generations” (Leviticus 24:3). It must be understood: And does God require its light for illumination at night? Didn’t the children of Israel, all forty years that they walked in the wilderness, walk exclusively by His light, the pillar of fire? Rather, the lighting of the candelabrum is testimony to mankind that the Divine Presence rests among Israel. The Gemara asks: What is this…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 10, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 22b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and they stated (Shabbat 22b) regarding the Menorah: "It is testimony to all inhabitants of the world that the Shechinah rests in Israel." And according to our words mentioned above that the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: Which is unique among the miracles not permitted to be written down in being established for all generations, for miracles not granted canonical scripture do not yet possess outward, corporeal manifestation, and they cannot be instituted for posterity each on its own. Rather, the miracle of Chanukah is the collective inclusion of all the unwritten miracles of the exile era, possessing a permanent observance for future generations exclusively through the kindling of the lamp.
column15: Meaning that regarding Shabbat as well, had it embodied the absolute divine Will directly without mediation, Shabbat could never be overridden for the preservation of life (pikuach nefesh)—for how could saving a life supersede the supreme divine Will?

column11: Ecclesiastes 4:12: ‘Also, if someone attacks, two can withstand it. A threefold cord is not readily broken!’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 11, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Ecclesiastes 4:12) to illuminate his exposition here (“and in the Responsa of the Maharil (end of Section 40) it states that he concluded: "To fulfill that which is stated: 'And a three-ply cord is not quickly severed'", and he concluded on this with...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column12: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:36 (§4)
column13: For it is not termed 'first' except when it coincides with the spring; since the beginning of the lunar months is validated only when spring arrives in the solar cycle, because the entire luminance of the moon exists through uniting with the sun and receiving from it. And it is known that the mystical secret of sun and moon alludes to the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, for the Congregation of Israel has no light of its own, receiving solely what they draw from Hashem, blessed be He.
column15: Meaning, because Nimrod observed the conclusion of the Flood taking place in Shinar, as stated in Zevachim (113b): Why was it called Shinar? Because all the corpses of the Flood were shaken out (nin'aru) there.

column11: Menachot 43b: ‘The baraita continues: Do you say that a garment with four corners is obligated but not a garment with three corners? Or is it teaching only that a garment with four corners is obligated but not a garment that has five corners? When the verse states: “With which you cover yourself,” a garment with five corners is thereby mentioned in the verse as being obligated. Then how do I realize the meaning of: “On the four corners of your garment”? It teaches that this obligation is limited to a garment that has four corners, but not to one that has three corners.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Menachot 43b) to illuminate his exposition here (“And behold in the Gemara (Menachot 43b) it states: "Whoever has tefillin on his head, tefillin on his arm, tzitzit on his garment, and a mezuzah on his doorway, all is in reinforcement that he...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: The purpose of “that you may look upon it, and remember all the commandments...” Numbers 15:39: the sky-blue thread tekhelet resembles the heavens Menachot 43b, and moralists wrote that gazing upon the expanse of the sky instills awe: “When I behold Your heavens... what is man that You are mindful of him?” Psalms 8:4–5; and it is said: “that His fear may be before you, that you sin not” Exodus 20:17.
column15: “And if you do not well, sin crouches at the door”—meaning: if you do not refine yourself now and wait until the threshold of the grave, there you can no longer refine yourself, for there sin crouches.

column11: Shabbat 89b: ‘And furthermore, how much did they actually sin? How long is a person’s life? Seventy years. Subtract the first twenty years of his life. One is not punished for sins committed then, as in heavenly matters, a person is only punished from age twenty. Fifty years remain for them. Subtract twenty-five years of nights, and twenty-five years remain for them. Subtract twelve and a half years during which one prays and eats and uses the bathroom, and twelve and a half years remain for them. If You can endure them all and forgive the sins committed during those years, excellent. And if not, half of the sins are upon me to bear and half upon You. And if You say that all of them, the sins of all…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 89b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and then is not the typical time to sin, as written (Shabbat 89b): "Subtract twenty-five [years] of nights", so that it does not fit that this mitzvah would protect from sin, especially since it...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: Then the 'beginning of dispute' became revealed, while the serpent—the husk of hatred and jealousy—was still wound around its heel. Its essential claim was indeed a dispute for the sake of Heaven: Korah argued, 'the entire congregation are all holy,' and therefore no one should exalt himself over the others. From the perspective of the future attainment, this is entirely true, as it is said: 'They shall no longer teach each man his fellow... for they shall all know Me,' etc.
column15: And this corresponds in man to the years of childhood up to age thirteen, during which he lacks mature intellect and no manifest Heavenly honor is discernible from his deeds—this state being termed “the heritage of nations”.

column11: Bereshit Rabbah 68: ‘“He dreamed, and behold, a ladder was set on the earth, its top was reaching the heavens, and behold, the angels of God were ascending and descending on it” (Genesis 28:12). “He dreamed, and behold, a ladder” – Rabbi Abbahu said: The content of dreams has no effect.). There was a certain person who came before Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥalafta. He said to him: ‘I saw in my dream that they were saying to me: Go and inherit your father’s business in Cappadocia.’ He said to him: ‘Has your father ever gone to Cappadocia?’ He said to him: ‘No.’ He said to him: ‘Go and count twenty beams in the roof of your house and you will find it.’ He said to him: ‘There are not twenty of them.’ He said to him: ‘If…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 11, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 68) to illuminate his exposition here (“like this rope which is not severed with fewer than three strands (Bereishit Rabbah 68); and this spiritual power is established and completed through the Chanukah lights across all souls of...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: With one or two strands the cord can still tear and be severed, though it is in truth a single extended cord. Thus the first and second strands themselves are strengthened against breaking by the addition of the third. Understand this well. In the dimension of time, this corresponds to the sanctity of Purim, the days of erasing Amalek, the descendant of Esau.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 18:2
column15: And that is: behold, at the hour the human form is born into the world, the divine point granted within him from Hashem is in smallness, contracted without any expansion; yet as he matures and acquires holiness for himself, the holiness begins expanding progressively more each time, acquiring for himself a house, field, vineyard, servants, and manifold possessions, and fathering sons and daughters, all of which broaden human intellect.

column11: Sotah 27b: ‘On that same day Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hyrcanus taught: Job served the Holy One, Blessed be He, only out of love, as it is stated: “Though He will slay me, still I will trust in Him” (Job 13:15). And still, the matter is even, i.e., the verse is ambiguous, as there are two possible interpretations of the verse. Was Job saying: I will await Him, expressing his yearning for God; or should the verse be interpreted as saying I will not await Him. As the word “lo” can mean either “to him” or “not,” it is unclear which meaning is intended here. This dilemma is resolved elsewhere, where the verse states a clearer indication of Job’s intent: “Till I die I will not put away my integrity from me”…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sotah 27b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and we find (Sotah 27b) where they derived that Job served solely out of love, as it is said: "Though He slay me, yet will I trust in Him until I die, etc."”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: It is known that the permission to hate one in whom a sinful matter is witnessed applies only to the evil itself; one must still love him for the good that is within him. We are commanded to separate even wicked people from transgression; the principle 'feed it to the wicked one,' etc., is said only when he is specifically wicked regarding that very matter, as I have written elsewhere.
column15: Indeed, it says “the glory of kings is to search out a matter” — meaning, since Hashem desired to bestow goodness upon His creatures and willed that finite creation should internalize His divine light, He deliberately structured creation to be bounded by limits and measure. However, from Hashem’s true vantage point there is neither limit nor measure, for in truth He is living, enduring, boundless, and infinite, and creation exists in utter perfection.

column11: Kiddushin 81a: ‘When he was halfway up the ladder, he strengthened his legs against the sides of the ladder to stop himself from climbing further, raised his voice, and cried out: There is a fire in the house of Amram. Upon hearing this, the Sages came and found him in that position. They said to him: You have embarrassed us, since everyone sees what you had intended to do. Rav Amram said to them: It is better that you be shamed in Amram’s house in this world, and not be ashamed of him in the World-to-Come. He took an oath that his evil inclination should emerge from him, and an apparition similar to a pillar of fire emerged from him. He said to his evil inclination: See, as you are fire and I am mere…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Kiddushin 81a) to illuminate his exposition here (“as written (Kiddushin 81a): "See that you are fire". And this is the power of the Oral Torah concerning which it is stated: "Is not My word like fire", because it issues from awe in the heart, as...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And this is astonishing in my eyes: since during that initial hour the fire in any event holds dominion to burn them and they suffer, as evidenced by the fact that they weep, shed tears, and justify the divine decree; and perforce it means that the fire lacks dominion to consume them into annihilation, as I wrote above; if so, what practical difference is there between suffering one hour and ascending immediately versus suffering twelve months, since ultimately the fire does not dominate to annihilate them?
column15: Meaning that upon reaching the boundary he should remind himself of the holy light of the Sabbath, pulling back his feet from extending any further outward, and returning to the inception, to the source whence he departed.

column11: Berakhot 17a: ‘Rava was wont to say: The objective of Torah wisdom is to achieve repentance and good deeds; that one should not read the Torah and study mishna and become arrogant and spurn his father and his mother and his teacher and one who is greater than he in wisdom or in the number of students who study before him, as it is stated: “The beginning of wisdom is fear of the Lord, a good understanding have all who fulfill them” (Psalms 111:10). It is not stated simply: All who fulfill, but rather: All who fulfill them, those who perform these actions as they ought to be performed, meaning those who do such deeds for their own sake, for the sake of the deeds themselves, not those who do them not for…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 17a) to illuminate his exposition here (“as stated: "Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom", – and as written (Berachot 17a): "The goal of wisdom is repentance and good deeds, etc., as it is said: 'The beginning of wisdom is the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And the eating of maror imparts holiness to all vegetable foods, and the eating of consecrated sacrificial meat imparts holiness to all meat; and therefore in our present era an unlettered boor (am ha'aretz) is forbidden to eat meat, because we lack sacrificial meat over which we recite the blessing "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us," except for Torah scholars, who do not need external actions to sanctify their bodies, for they themselves are holy.
column15: Just as one standing before the king is utterly self-nullified from awe, such that an observer behind him sees no movement of life, and only when he turns his face outward do his actions become manifest.

column11: Berakhot 17a: ‘Rava was wont to say: The objective of Torah wisdom is to achieve repentance and good deeds; that one should not read the Torah and study mishna and become arrogant and spurn his father and his mother and his teacher and one who is greater than he in wisdom or in the number of students who study before him, as it is stated: “The beginning of wisdom is fear of the Lord, a good understanding have all who fulfill them” (Psalms 111:10). It is not stated simply: All who fulfill, but rather: All who fulfill them, those who perform these actions as they ought to be performed, meaning those who do such deeds for their own sake, for the sake of the deeds themselves, not those who do them not for…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 17a) to illuminate his exposition here (“and as written (Berachot 17a): "The goal of wisdom is repentance and good deeds, etc., as it is said: 'The beginning of wisdom is the fear of Hashem'". And Isaac's aspect, who was the chariot for...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: In the Gemara, Berakhot 17a: The World to Come contains neither eating nor drinking, as stated in Midrash Kohelet 2:24: every biblical reference to eating and drinking refers to Torah and good deeds; and as written in Avodah Zarah 5a: tomorrow in the afterlife is not the time to perform them. "Rather, the righteous sit" Berakhot 17a—and do not walk, like stationary angels who stand possessing no knee-joints to bend their legs, as noted in the Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 1:1.
column15: The meaning of this is: when Hashem shows a person that He validates and grants space to his divine service, the person must then serve Hashem with even greater humility and must not assume personal pride or assertiveness simply because Hashem revealed that his toil holds significance; rather, he must labor, fence himself in, and constrict his ego even further, recognizing that there is no independent perfection in creation, but that true perfection resides solely with Hashem.

column11: Tikkunei Zohar 42b:2-63a:9: ‘(Ruth 3:13) ... as Y”Y lives lie down until the morning, which is the right-side, in which is the power of the Written Torah, which is the Middle Pillar, for the Written Torah is given from the right-side, and from the left-side is given the Oral Torah, which is ‘female’. And because of this ‘good’, the Righteous-One, ‘the life-force of the worlds’, is from the left-hand side, for it is ‘the mighty-one who conquers his evil inclination’ – which is Samael.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 11, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Tikkunei Zohar 42b:2-63a:9) to illuminate his exposition here (“and it states in the Zohar and Tikunim (mentioned above, discourse 1): "From the right was given the Written Torah, and from the left was given the Oral Torah", and further: "And when it is taken...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: For Yom HaKippurim, as stated in the Tikkunei Zohar (Tikkun 21), is like Purim (Yom Ke-Purim), and which is dependent upon which? The lesser upon the greater (Ta'anit 7a), making Purim greater than Yom Kippur; meaning that Yom Kippur corresponds to the World of Understanding (Binah), as is known, at which time the Holy One, blessed be He, was reconciled over the sin of the Golden Calf, commanding thereupon the construction of the Mishkan and the offerings which had not been commanded prior.
column15: And afterward, when habitual sin hardens until he acts without pleasure merely out of cold routine, it returns to the male force, deeply rooted, upon which the Zohar says: “and transforms against him like a mighty warrior.” And indeed so it is.

column11: Chagigah 27a: ‘§ Apropos the coating of the altar, the Gemara cites an Aggadic teaching: Rabbi Abbahu said that Rabbi Elazar said: The fire of Gehenna has no power over Torah scholars. This can be derived by an a fortiori inference from the salamander [salamandra], a creature created out of fire and immune to its effects, and whose blood is fireproof: If a salamander, which is merely a product of fire, and nevertheless when one anoints his body with its blood, fire has no power over him, all the more so should fire not have any power over Torah scholars, whose entire bodies are fire, as it is written: “Surely My words are as fire, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 23:29), and the words of Torah become part of…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Chagigah 27a) to illuminate his exposition here (“and so they said (end of Chagigah 27a): "Torah scholars whose entire body is fire, etc.", which is the Oral Torah, a fire consuming the fire of the Evil Inclination. And to this alludes the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And likewise, one who cleaves to the Torah and contemplates it constantly, all his limbs become transformed into it, as our Sages of blessed memory stated (end of Chagigah 27a): the fire of Gehenna has no dominion over Torah scholars, for their entire body is fire, as it is said: "Is not My word like as fire?" (Jeremiah 23:29). And so it is with every single character trait.
column15: The meaning is: the eyes of Atika continually gaze with unblinking openness upon the divine Will, acknowledging that all strength is solely from Hashem, no creature holding power to alter the supreme Will.

column11: Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5: ‘“I came to my garden, my sister, my bride; I gathered my myrrh with my perfume; I ate my honeycomb with my honey; I drank my wine with my milk. Eat, friends; drink abundantly, beloved ones” (Song of Songs 5:1).“I came to my garden” – Rabbi Menaḥem, son-in-law of Rabbi Elazar bar Avuna, said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi Yosena: It is not written here, “I came to a garden,” but rather “to my garden [legani]” – to My wedding canopy [leginuni], to the place that was the site of My initial appearance. Was not the first appearance of the Divine Presence in the lower realm? That is what is written: “They heard the voice of the Lord God moving about in the garden” (Genesis 3:8). Rabbi…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 11, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5) to illuminate his exposition here (“following what is written (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5) on the verse "Open to me": "Open for Me a single opening of repentance like the eye of a needle, and I will open for you entrances through which...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And then he needed to direct his heart to stabilize his thoughts properly, yet it did not avail since from Heaven they disturbed him. And so with the other Amoraim mentioned there—it was at an hour when distraction was brought upon them from Heaven so that deliberate effort was required. But ordinarily they required no deliberate effort at all, their heart crying out spontaneously to Hashem during prayer, as is true of anyone free from delusion.
column15: And whenever a person does not see clearly the Heavenly glory rising from a situation, the mind of man becomes deeply distressed; for in a place where a person perceives the divine glory that can yet be revealed, he is not so perturbed. But at sea, where it appears that “His glory is not found,” human consciousness is thrown into agitation.

column11: Gittin 56a: ‘The Roman authorities then sent Vespasian Caesar against the Jews. He came and laid siege to Jerusalem for three years. There were at that time in Jerusalem these three wealthy people: Nakdimon ben Guryon, ben Kalba Savua, and ben Tzitzit HaKesat. The Gemara explains their names: Nakdimon ben Guryon was called by that name because the sun shined [nakad] on his behalf, as it is related elsewhere (see Ta’anit 19b) that the sun once continued to shine in order to prevent him from suffering a substantial loss. Ben Kalba Savua was called this because anyone who entered his house when he was hungry as a dog [kelev] would leave satiated [save’a]. Ben Tzitzit HaKesat was referred to by that name…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 11, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Gittin 56a) to illuminate his exposition here (“and from his descendants descended Nero who converted (Gittin 56a). And this is what is stated (Targum Yonatan, Parashat Vayechi): "That the head of Esau was placed inside the bosom of Isaac", and...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: That is, there in the “heel” is hidden the “beginning of thought” and the root of David — corresponding to the World of Asiyah [Action], which is the perfection of the deed. — so that the very lowest “heel,” where Esav took hold, is precisely where the root of David lay hidden, and whence Mashiach will yet rise.
column15: Therefore his punishment was that he was castrated after a time—meaning that no enduring spiritual remnant for eternal life remained from him for his descendants after him, but only a temporary existence for the six thousand years of this world.

column11: Targum Jonathan on Genesis 50:13: “Targum Jonathan on Genesis 50:13 relates that when the sons of Jacob brought their father to be buried in the Cave of Machpelah, Esau the wicked came to prevent them; Chushim the son of Dan, who was hard of hearing, struck off Esau’s head with his sword, and Esau’s head rolled into the cave and came to rest in the bosom of Isaac while his body was sent back to Mount Seir.” Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 11, Rav Tzadok cites this commentary and philosophical-halakhic exposition (Targum Jonathan on Genesis 50:13) to illuminate his exposition here (“And this is what is stated (Targum Yonatan, Parashat Vayechi): "That the head of Esau was placed inside the bosom of Isaac", and his head was buried in the Cave of Machpelah, see there. And he is...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: This brings about the erasure of Esau and Amalek. Amalek is the root of Esau's evil, descending from Eliphaz, who was among the prophets of the nations and dwelt in the tents of our father Jacob, peace be upon him. Eliphaz had absorbed the good inherited by Esau from the Patriarchs. Timna likewise desired to cleave to the seed of the Patriarchs, but because she came from the evil root of Seir she attached herself to him, in whom Esau's root was present.
column14: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:9 (§2)
column15: And when they join as a single assembly unto Hashem, then one radiates of his holiness into his fellow, and his fellow into him, and consequently, even if there exists some defect in an individual, nonetheless no prosecuting accusation can alight upon them, since the other completes this deficiency, being himself refined in that very trait, and as explained in Parashat Nitzavim.

column11: Ecclesiastes 1:18: ‘For as wisdom grows, vexation grows;To increase learning is to increase heartache.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 12, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Ecclesiastes 1:18) to illuminate his exposition here (“for abundant wisdom radiates even upon the abundant grief of the foolish heart (as explained in discourse 10); and this is delightful and pleasant before Him as we explained, and this is why it...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: In proportion to the preeminence of knowledge and wisdom within a person, so do illusions surge corresponding to them in his mind and heart, in the manner of: "he that increases knowledge increases sorrow" (Ecclesiastes 1:18). And so with the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil: through good knowledge entering him, its opposite entered as well, as written in Sotah 21b: once wisdom enters, cunning enters, as it is said: "I, wisdom, dwell with prudence/cunning" (Proverbs 8:12).
column15: Meaning, even prior to divine illumination when a person still dwells in darkness, if his heart yearns passionately for redemption, holy counsel emerges within him allowing worldly goods to elevate his service.

column11: Ramban on Numbers 8:2: “‘Speak unto Aaron, and say unto him: When you light the lamps, the seven lamps shall give light in front of the candlestick’ (Numbers 8:2): Ramban quotes the Midrash Rabbah that Hashem comforted Aaron when he saw the dedication offerings of the twelve tribal Princes, promising him: ‘By your life, yours is greater than theirs—for the sacrifices operate only while the Temple stands, whereas your lamps (referring to the Hasmonean dedication of the Chanukah lights) will shine forever.’” Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 12, Rav Tzadok cites this commentary and philosophical-halakhic exposition (Ramban on Numbers 8:2) to illuminate his exposition here (“as the Ramban wrote regarding what is stated (in Midrash Rabbah, Beha'alotecha): "However the lights are forever", alluding to the Chanukah light, see there, and as we have explained.”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And all deeds of King David achieved their visible actualization through his son Solomon; as with the Temple whose dedication was attributed unto David, he being the builder in potential; issuing into deed afterward through Solomon solely by virtue of David's foundational strength. Wherefore the essence of the building is named after David, while its practical execution was through King Solomon; it not being fitting to become manifest until Solomon arrived who issued from his essence and power.
column15: Concerning beasts, however, this was not stated, but merely “green herb,” which leaves no enduring seed-remnant but is strictly temporary, just as the beast's animal soul is merely for the hour, possessing no eternal life.

column11: Pesikta Rabbati 4:1: “‘And Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, unto whom the word of the Lord came, saying: Israel shall be your name’ (I Kings 18:31): The Pesikta links Elijah’s twelve-stone altar with Rosh Chodesh and Chanukah, teaching that Elijah restores the unity of the twelve tribes and the covenantal light of the altar.” Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 13, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Pesikta Rabbati 4:1) to illuminate his exposition here (“– In the Pesikta (Parashah 4) for Chanukah: "'And Elijah took twelve stones' — may it be favorable when Rosh Chodesh falls on Chanukah, etc., you find, etc." From the arrangement of the Pesikta it...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And this is the consummate perfection of the Name Havayah, as is known that the first two letters (Yud-Hei) represent the fathers [Chochmah and Binah], and the last two letters (Vav-Hei) represent the offspring [Middos and Malchus]; and through this is accomplished the shattering (giddud) of the foundation of the nations of the world, through whose existence the Divine Name remains incomplete; and the letters of the spelled-out filling (milui) are likewise termed "children" relative to the primary letters which are the fathers giving birth to them.
column15: In that the Blessed Name possesses exact measure, knowing how much light to impart to this generation and how much to another according to each one’s capacity; and this is “with the Holy One the matter is bound.”

column11: Megillah 31a: ‘The baraita continues: On each day of Hanukkah they read a selection from the portion of the dedication of the altar by the tribal princes (Numbers 7), and they read as the haftara from the portion of the lamps of Zechariah (Zechariah 2:14–4:7). The Gemara comments: And if it occurs that there are two Shabbatot during Hanukkah, on the first Shabbat they read from the portion of the lamps of Zechariah, and on the latter one they read from the portion of the lamps of Solomon (I Kings 7:40–50), which discusses the lamps in the Temple.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 13, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Megillah 31a) to illuminate his exposition here (“for granted the lamps of Zechariah and the lamps of Solomon which we read as Haftarah according to the Gemara (Megillah 31a) are related to Chanukah, since the miracle was likewise in the Temple...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: Meaning, they reach the realization that the Blessed Name is infinitely set apart, transcendent, and exalted beyond created mortal intellect, which is consummate comprehension. Wherefore the Sages taught (Megillah 31a): Wherever you find the greatness of the Holy One, blessed be He, there you find His humility; for in the very dimension where Hashem's transcendent majesty is apprehended by a creature, there His humility shines by allowing Himself to be grasped even by a lowly mortal, since by perceiving His transcendence the creature grasps Hashem, which is the zenith of comprehension for a created being.
column15: And as taught in the Gemara (Megillah 19b): Had there remained in the cave where Moses and Elijah stood even an opening the size of the eye of a fine needle, they would have been unable to survive before the brilliance of that illumination.

column11: Bereshit Rabbah 82: ‘Rabbi Yudan, Rabbi Aivu, and Rabbi Mashyan ben Nagari said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan: [God told Jacob:] ‘Your descendants are destined to become a nation like the assembly of peoples; just as the assembly of peoples sacrifice [on private altars] at the time when the private altars are prohibited, so, your descendants will sacrifice at the time when the private altars are prohibited.’). And the "let them play" of Abner was likewise so, as is known that they were heads of Sanhedrin, and as written (Bereishit Rabbah 82) that Abner expounded the verse "kings shall come out of your loins" and coronated Ish-bosheth, and his warfare was waged through words of Torah— to triumph through Torah proof that the halakhah agreed with him regarding the reign of Ish-bosheth.
column15: And as stated by the holy Ari, of blessed memory (Likutei Torah, Parashat Bereishit, s.v. Vayomer HaAdam Zot HaPa'am), the letters of the spelling-out (millui) of the Name of 45 are numerically equal to Chavah .

column11: Zohar, Vaera 4:53-54: ‘Then came the promise of redemption, namely, that He would not merely free them from Egypt and then leave them to themselves: this was followed by the proclamation that He would make them His people; and finally came the promise that He would bring them into their own land (v. 7).’’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 13, Rav Tzadok cites this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Vaera 4:53-54) to illuminate his exposition here (“as written in Ra'aya Meheimna (Zohar Part II, 25a): "And at the end of forty years, etc., then he taught them in an individualized manner, this is what is written: 'And you shall know this day,...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: And therefore the letter Yud encompasses the entire Name from the perspective of whatever perception is manifest to human beings; while the Aleph is the transcendent root of Ayin concealed from all thought, wherefore the letter Aleph is silent and unvoiced in pronunciation; wherefore it is the inception of all speech, as written in Ma'ayan HaChochmah: from the mere opening of the mouth alone the letter Aleph is formed; for vocal speech is the manifestation ex nihilo from the concealed depths of the heart.
column15: So that creation would not dissolve out of existence from the intensity of the light of Havayah, collapsing back into its Source like the shattered worlds that fell prior to this world due to an excess of unmediated light.

column11: Berakhot 54a: ‘The mishna articulates a general principle: One is obligated to recite a blessing for the bad that befalls him just as he recites a blessing for the good that befalls him, as it is stated: “And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:5). The mishna explains this verse as follows: “With all your heart” means with your two inclinations, with your good inclination and your evil inclination, both of which must be subjugated to the love of God. “With all your soul” means even if God takes your soul. “And with all your might” means with all your money, as money is referred to in the Bible as might. Alternatively, it may…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 13, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 54a) to illuminate his exposition here (“as expounded (in Chapter HaRo'eh, Berachot 54a) on "with all your heart"; for Havayah, which shows that everything is unified as prior to the world's creation, in this we have no sensory grasp in...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.

column13: Execution having been decreed against him by Pharaoh, he was spared through exile, as in repentance where willful sins become errors and then merits (Yoma 86b). For from that exile Hashem appeared to him at Mount Horeb, which drew Moses as a lodestone draws metal (Zohar II, 21a). And specifically through exile he reached that mountain, nothing occurring by chance, meriting that sanctuary through his wandering [after the teaching: "Who is wise? He who recognizes his place" (Avot 6:6), attaining sublime wisdom].
column15: And whoever takes from that which is not of his own kind—that offspring who is compounded of both—of him it is said, “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk,” etc.; for that offspring who is compounded of both is a mixture, kilayim, issuing from a woman who is not of his kind, who is opposite him.

column11: Shir HaShirim Rabbah 7:5: ‘“…your nose is as the tower of Lebanon…” (Shir HaShirim 7:5) This refers to the Holy Temple. Just as the nose is placed at the highpoint of a person, so too the Holy Temple is placed at the highpoint of the world. Just as the majority of decorations are hung from the nose, so to the priests, levites and kings are from Yaakov. ‘as the tower of Lebanon.’ As it says “…this good mountain and the Lebanon.” (Devarim 3:25) R’ Teviyumi said ‘it bleaches out (malbin) the sins of Israel like snow, as it says “…If your sins prove to be like crimson, they will become white as snow…” (Yeshayahu 1:18) R’ Shimon bar Yochai says ‘because all hearts (levavot) rejoice in it, as it says “The fairest of…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 13, Rav Tzadok cites this midrashic exposition (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 7:5) to illuminate his exposition here (“And it states (Shir HaShirim Rabbah, Parashah 7) on the verse "Your head upon you is like Carmel": "The destitute (rashim) within you are as beloved to Me as Elijah who ascended Mount Carmel." And...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: When even the lowliest pauper in Israel will be like Eliyahu, as written in Shir HaShirim Rabbah (7:6) on the verse "Your head upon you is like Carmel" (Shir HaShirim 7:6). And this world is filled with contention, yet Hashem did not cast Peace to the earth, but cast Truth to the earth, as written in Bereishis Rabbah (8:5); for in truth, from the perspective of absolute Truth there is no division or discord; but solely because Truth is concealed in this world, its goodness hidden within it.
column15: Because they lived immediately following the dawn of creation, there was a profound tension: just yesterday the Blessed Name was termed “He” (Hu)—transcendent and concealed—and now He was to be addressed directly as “You” (Attah).

column11: Shabbat 89b: ‘We learned in the mishna: From where is it derived that one ties a scarlet strip of wool to the scapegoat? As it says: “If your sins be like scarlet [kashanim], they will become white like snow” (Isaiah 1:18). The Gemara wonders at this: Why does the verse use the plural form: Kashanim? It should have used the singular form: Kashani. Rabbi Yitzḥak said that the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to the Jewish people: Even if your sins are as numerous as those years [kashanim] that have proceeded continuously from the six days of Creation until now, they will become white like snow. Rava taught: What is the meaning of that which is written: “Go please and let us reason together, the Lord will…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 13, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 89b) to illuminate his exposition here (“then the Blessed Name clarifies, as written (Shabbat 89b): – "Though your sins be like scarlet (shanim) — like these years (shanim) ordered from the Six Days of Creation until now", meaning that...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: For behold the matter of Isaac seeking to bless Esau: could it enter your mind that Rebecca knew Jacob was a tzaddik and Esau wicked, while Isaac was ignorant?! Rather, this was the entire essence of Isaac: to intercede even for the wicked among his seed that they perish not; as stated in Shabbat (89b): that Abraham and Jacob responded to Hashem regarding sinners, "let them be erased, etc."; while Isaac pleaded on behalf of the transgressors of Israel, accepting upon himself their punishment: "half is upon me, etc."
column15: And it does not suffice for man merely to repair what occurred from the time of his own creation, but from the very dawn of genesis the Blessed Name embedded an intentional void within creation, so that man through holy toil should complete that lack.

column11: Makkot 23b: ‘The Gemara cites a somewhat similar statement. Rabbi Elazar says: In three places the Divine Spirit appeared before all to affirm that the action taken was appropriate: In the court of Shem, in the court of Samuel the Ramathite, and in the court of Solomon. The Gemara elaborates: This occurred in the court of Shem, as it is written in the context of the episode of Judah and Tamar: “And Judah acknowledged them and said: She is more righteous than I [mimmenni]” (Genesis 38:26). How did Judah know that Tamar’s assertion that she was bearing his child was correct? Perhaps, just as he went to her and hired her as a prostitute, another person went to her and hired her as well, and he is not…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 13, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Makkot 23b) to illuminate his exposition here (“after the manner of the Heavenly Voice that proclaimed regarding Judah: "From Me these hidden matters emerged" (Makkot 23b); and then "they shall become white as snow", meaning not merely that...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.

column15: And behold, when Hashem bestows His influx, namely during conception and birth, even though man is in self-forgetfulness and concealment, nonetheless he need not fear then, since from Him, blessed be He, matters emerge governed and directed; as we find regarding Judah where Hashem declared (Genesis 38:26): “She is more righteous than I—from Me the matter came.”

column11: Yoma 86b: ‘Reish Lakish said: Great is repentance, as the penitent’s intentional sins are counted for him as unwitting transgressions, as it is stated: “Return, Israel, to the Lord your God, for you have stumbled in your iniquity” (Hosea 14:2). The Gemara analyzes this: Doesn’t “iniquity” mean an intentional sin? Yet the prophet calls it stumbling, implying that one who repents is considered as though he only stumbled accidentally in his transgression. The Gemara asks: Is that so? Didn’t Reish Lakish himself say: Great is repentance, as one’s intentional sins are counted for him as merits, as it is stated: “And when the wicked turns from his wickedness, and does that which is lawful and right, he…’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 13, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Yoma 86b) to illuminate his exposition here (“and this occurs through repentance from love, wherein intentional transgressions become merits (Yoma 86b, and explained often). And Scripture linked this to Elijah, for this spiritual power...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: In human perception, a penitent (ba'al teshuvah) is not equal to a wholly righteous person (tzadik gamur), and it goes without saying that the sins he committed previously would not be considered as merits, even though one believes in the words of our Sages that willful sins become like merits (Yoma 86b), and they also said (Berakhot 34b): "In the place where penitents stand, the wholly righteous cannot stand" and the one who disputes this does so regarding the comprehension of the prophets, where one master derives from the verse 'to him that is far off and to him that is near' (Isaiah 57:19) which is among the prophets, and in his view it is not so from…

column15: For Avraham our Father introduced even into this world that all know from small to great that there exists a Creator in the universe, a living and enduring God Who supervises all particulars, and Avraham's entire longing was solely for eternal life, contracting himself wherever he trod in order to attain eternal life through this.

column15: A priest is the conduit through whom all blessings and divine flows are channeled; wherefore when Malki-Tzedek saw that Avraham our Father was now the chosen one to minister to Hashem, through whom the influxes would flow— he brought forth bread and wine, to hint to him that now Avraham is the sum of all influxes and the central conduit; for bread and wine encompass the totality of all divine sustenance.

column13: And the root of the revelation of Keser Elyon, concealed from every creature in this world, is in the letter Yud alluding to the inception of existence ex nihilo from Ayin; and within the upper thorn of the Yud is hinted Ayin [Nothingness]; for the perception of Ayin is achieved through the Yesh [Being], which is Chochmah grasped within human intellect; and through the existence of Yesh mortals know that there exists a transcendent Ayin that creates that Yesh, wherefore Ayin is indicated in the thorn of the Yud.

And one who perceives the essential melody that the sun chants unto Hashem, that person will not consider the physical light of the sun as primary at all, for he knows that the root of everything is the song and praise, which is an influx from Hashem.

column11: Berakhot 18b: ‘In contrast to the righteous, who are referred to as living even after their death, the verse states explicitly: “The dead know nothing.” These are the wicked, who even during their lives are called dead, as the prophet Ezekiel said in reference to a king of Israel who was alive: “And you are a slain, wicked prince of Israel” (Ezekiel 21:30). And if you wish, say instead that the proof is from here: “At the mouth of two witnesses or three witnesses the dead shall be put to death” (Deuteronomy 17:6). This is puzzling. As long as the accused has not been sentenced to death, he is alive. Rather, this person who is wicked is considered dead from the outset.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 13, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 18b) to illuminate his exposition here (“the wicked who in their lifetimes are called "dead" as written (Berachot 18b), and he will bring them back in repentance and grant them spiritual life, and this too is an aspect of the...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: 16 (§4): And therefore the Sages taught (Berakhot 18b): the wicked in their lifetimes are called dead, for genuine life issues from the soul; but if one cleaves to corporeal lusts of the body, his soul-faculties remain mere shadows, and he is termed dead, just as upon the departure of his soul he is physically dead. But one who cleaves to Hashem God of Truth—which our Sages expounded (Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 1:1; Bereishit Rabbah 81:2; Vayikra Rabbah 26:1): why is He called Truth? Because He is the living God and eternal King.
column15: Therefore the Blessed Name commanded us to guard these boundaries, and through this comes “I will feed you the heritage of Jacob”—an unbounded heritage, because you are cleaving to Him who is infinite and limitless.

column11: Jerusalem Talmud Shekalim 3:3: “Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair taught: Torah leads to watchfulness; watchfulness leads to alacrity; alacrity leads to cleanliness; cleanliness leads to abstinence; abstinence leads to purity; purity leads to piety (chasidut); humility leads to fear of sin; fear of sin leads to holiness; holiness leads to the Holy Spirit (Ruach HaKodesh); and the Holy Spirit leads to the Resurrection of the Dead—and humility is greatest of them all.” Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 13, Rav Tzadok cites this scriptural verse (Jerusalem Talmud Shekalim 3:3) to illuminate his exposition here (“And in the Yerushalmi (end of Chapter 3 of Shekalim) they stated: "Piety leads to Divine Inspiration, as it is written: 'Then You spoke in a vision to Your pious ones'; Divine Inspiration leads to...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.
column13: Meriting likewise the Crown of Priesthood, he having been consecrated a Kohen as mentioned. And likewise the name Eliyahu contains the three distinct letters of the Name Havayah and the Name Ehyeh (Aleph-Yud-Hei-Vav), excluding the doubled letter Hei which is not a separate letter; for in truth the letter Vav, which is the Central Pillar extending from one end to the other, encompasses the entire Name from the Yud; and so too the Yud of Ehyeh which is a simple point encompasses the whole Name, for all Hebrew letters are formed from a primal point.

column11: Ketubot 111b: ‘Rabbi Yoḥanan said to Rabbi Elazar: Their master, i.e. God, is not pleased that you say this of ordinary Jews. Rather, that verse is written about one who weakens himself and succumbs to idol worship. Those who commit this great sin do not merit to be resurrected in the future. column11: Taanit 7a: ‘Similarly, Rav Yehuda said: The day of the rains is as great as the day on which the Torah was given, as it is stated: “My doctrine [likḥi] shall drop as the rain” (Deuteronomy 32:2), and lekaḥ means nothing other than Torah, as it is stated: “For I give you good doctrine [lekaḥ]; do not forsake My Torah” (Proverbs 4:2). column11: Taanit 7a: ‘Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa raised a contradiction. In one verse it is written: “To him who is thirsty bring water” (Isaiah 21:14), which indicates that the one who has water must bring it to the thirsty person, and it is written elsewhere: “Ho, everyone who thirsts, come for water” (Isaiah 55:1), from which it may be inferred that the thirsty person must seek out water himself. Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa resolves this apparent contradiction by explaining that if he is a worthy student the teacher must seek him out, as in “to him who is thirsty bring water,” but if the student is not worthy, then “Ho, everyone who thirsts, come for water,” i.e., this student must seek out a teacher himself.’ Context and connection to Peri Tzadik: In Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 14, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Taanit 7a) to illuminate his exposition here (“regarding which they stated in the Gemara (Ta'anit 7a) that it is likened to water, alluding to: "Ho, everyone that thirsts, come to the waters", and stated: "Bring water to meet him that is...”), showing how the translated source sheds light on the inner dimensions of Torah and divine service developed in Peri Tzadik.

column11: Rosh Hashanah 30a: ‘Rather, is it not the case that in Jerusalem they sound the shofar both when the court was in session, i.e., until midday, and when the court was not in session.
